document_title: Anchorage Kept the 14 Days in Policy, Not Code
post_copy:
If you drive in Anchorage, a patrol car's plate reader can log your plate, and APD's own policy deletes it after 14 days.

An amendment to put that clock in city code was rejected. Alaska's News Source reports the ordinance passed 11 to 1.

Erin Baldwin Day's Amendment 12, passed unanimously, requires a memo to the Assembly 30 days before APD changes a storage limit. The filed text gave notice within 30 days after.

The Anchorage Daily News reports a committee will meet monthly for a year to recommend, not discipline, and that APD relies more on AI to aid investigations. The city chose notice over numbers.

Five votes from November 4th sit beside the notice rule as filed and as amended, the committee's limits and the filed AI definition.

Should shortening the 14 days take only a memo, and lengthening it take an Assembly vote?

#AnchorageAssembly #LicensePlateReaders #AlaskaAI

slides.headline: The surveillance rules passed 11 to 1.
slides.body: An amendment to write a 14-day deletion deadline into city code was rejected. APD already deletes plate reader data after 14 days, under its own department policy.
labels: VOTES PER ALASKA'S NEWS SOURCE · 14 DAYS PER APD

slides.kicker: THE WORDS IN PLACE OF A NUMBER
slides.headline: "articulable operational needs"
slides.body: Municipal Attorney Eva Gardner argued retention must stay adaptable on that standard, per Alaska's News Source. The substitute as filed September 15th used the same words and set no fixed number of days.

slides.headline: Thirty days of warning, now before the change.
slides.body: APD is required to give the Assembly 30 days of advance notice by memo before a material policy change, and a change to data storage limits counts.

slides.headline: A number in code takes an ordinance to change. A number in APD policy takes a memo and 30 days' notice.
November 4th, in five votes
labels: Amendment 5, a 14-day deletion deadline in code
Amendment 11, warrants for past plate searches
A temporary committee to oversee APD policies

slides.headline: A committee to watch the policies, monthly, for a year.
slides.body: At least four Assembly members, led by Kameron Perez-Verdia, meeting in public at least once a month, per the Anchorage Daily News. It can recommend changes, not discipline.
labels: ONE NOTCH PER MONTH, ONE YEAR

slides.headline: "machine learning, artificial intelligence, or similar technology"
slides.body: That is how the substitute as filed defined surveillance technology. The Anchorage Daily News reports APD now relies more on tools including artificial intelligence used to aid investigations.
labels: UP TO 750 CAMERAS, CRIME CENTER CAPACITY

Sources, primary first

Anchorage Assembly, AO 2026-108(S) as filed 2026-09-15, the mayor's substitute with its surveillance technology definition, the "articulable operational needs" standard and its 30-day notice clause, https://www.muni.org/Departments/Assembly/SiteAssets/Pages/focus-on-public-safety/13.C.3.--AO%202026-108%28S%29.pdf (the municipality's site returned not found for this PDF on November 5th, and the as-amended text that passed wasn't readable anywhere, so the deck describes the substitute as filed, quoting a reading of this PDF from October 10th)
Alaska's News Source (KTUU), by Jonson Kuhn, Anchorage Assembly passes police surveillance rules after rejecting stricter limits, the 11 to 1 final vote and Amendments 5, 11 and 12, 2026-11-05, https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/11/05/anchorage-assembly-passes-police-surveillance-rules-after-rejecting-stricter-limits/
Anchorage Daily News, by Chris Aadland, Anchorage Assembly approves temporary committee to oversee APD policies, the 10 to 1 committee vote and AI used to aid investigations, 2026-11-05, https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/anchorage/2026/11/05/anchorage-assembly-approves-temporary-committee-to-oversee-apd-policies/
Anchorage Daily News, by Zachariah Hughes, Anchorage Assembly delays vote on reformed surveillance rules, the October 20th meeting and AI in APD casework, 2026-10-26, https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/anchorage/2026/10/26/anchorage-assembly-delays-vote-on-reformed-surveillance-rules/
Alaska Public Media, by Wesley Early, Anchorage Assembly approves $600K police crime center upgrade, a crime center that could access up to 750 cameras at full capacity, 2026-09-03, https://alaskapublic.org/news/public-safety/2026-09-03/anchorage-assembly-approves-600k-police-crime-center-upgrade-holds-off-on-updating-privacy-protections
Alaska's News Source (KTUU), by Joe Allgood, Looking inside Anchorage police's Real-Time Crime Center, 238 cameras registered and 11 integrated with APD in late August, 2026-08-27, https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/08/28/looking-inside-anchorage-polices-real-time-crime-center/

Vote tallies are as reported by Alaska's News Source, and no tally was reported for Amendment 5, the 14-day amendment. The committee's 10 to 1 vote is as reported by the Anchorage Daily News. The letterboard on the slides is studio art showing the policy's number, not a photo of anything APD posts.

Every open Alaska AI decision on the docket, with its next deadline, is at https://alaskaaihq.com
Watched the November 4th meeting, or found the as-amended text posted publicly? Add context in the replies, with a public source where one exists.
aftercare: Post Tuesday November 10th to Thursday November 12th, 8 to 11 a.m. Alaska time. Drafts arrive daily and you decide when to post. Wednesday November 11th is Veterans Day, and feeds that day run to tributes, so Tuesday or Thursday may be the cleaner slot.
Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting and pin it, with every URL as plain text so LinkedIn keeps the links. The deck has no music or produced media, so there's no credits comment.

Reply to every comment in the first 90 minutes, with claims only and no first person. 'Did they drop the 14 days?' No. It remains APD policy, and APD's own page says scanned data is automatically deleted after 14 days (C35, C06). It just isn't in city code, because Amendment 5 was rejected (C05). 'Is the notice a veto?' No. Amendment 12 requires 30 days' advance notice by informational memorandum (C12, C13).

'Who voted no?' No source names the ordinance's lone no vote, so don't guess. Keith McCormick was the only no on the separate committee vote (C19). 'Does lengthening the 14 days need an Assembly vote today?' No claim says so. As reported, Amendment 12 treats any change to data storage limits, longer or shorter, as a trigger for 30 days' advance notice (C13); the caption's question is a proposal. 'Is APD using AI?' The Anchorage Daily News reports APD relies more on AI to aid investigations and doesn't name the tool (C27). APD's own page has no AI wording, and it says APD doesn't use facial recognition or Flock cameras (C34).
After 48 hours, note saves and comments for the ledger.
editor_notes_for_email: Every vote fact rests on one outlet, Alaska's News Source (KTUU, November 5th): the 11 to 1 final passage, the rejection of Amendment 5 with no tally, the 5 to 7 on Amendment 11 and the unanimous Amendment 12. No second outlet and no municipal record carried the vote, so the caption and slides 02, 04 and 06 attribute every tally. Every muni.org page and PDF returned 404 on November 5th, so the as-amended text is unread, and C44 to C51 are carried from the October 10th reading with fetched false; the deck uses only C44, C46, C47 and C48, each labelled as filed, and the 'after' in 'within thirty days after' (slide 04) is the fact-checker's reading of 'within 30 days of any material modification'. The AI hook rests on ADN's characterization (C27) and the as-filed definition (C44); APD's own page has no AI wording. The caption's closing question was reworded to read as a proposal ('Should shortening the 14 days take only a memo, and lengthening it take an Assembly vote?'), since no claim says lengthening needs a vote today.
